name: Appudaiyar Temple, Sellur (Thiru Aappanoor)
deity: Shiva as Appudaiyar (Annavinodhar), with the goddess Kuravankamazh Kuzhali
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Pandya Nadu on the Vaigai at Madurai, sung by Sambandar in the Tevaram (7th century)
dynasty: Pandya, enlarged under the Madurai Nayaks
summary: Across the Vaigai from old Madurai, at the Thiru Aappanoor of the Tevaram, Shiva is worshipped as Appudaiyar, the Lord who came to dwell in a simple wooden wedge for a hungry Pandya king.

sections.history: Sellur lies on the north bank of the Vaigai, facing the old city of Madurai across the river, and its Shiva temple is the Thiru Aappanoor of the Tevaram. It is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and is counted second among the fourteen of Pandya Nadu; Thirugnana Sambandar sang a pathigam to the Lord here during his stay in the Pandya capital. Tradition credits the Pandya kings with founding the shrine and the Madurai Nayaks with enlarging it, and the Sethupathis of Ramanathapuram are remembered among its patrons. Though it stands in the shadow of the great Meenakshi temple, it keeps its own place in the Shaiva story of Madurai.
sections.architecture: This is a modest neighbourhood temple rather than a towered complex. The entrance is crowned not by a tall gopuram but by a stucco group of Shiva and Parvati seated on the bull, Rishabharudar, and within, a walled enclosure gathers the sanctum of the lingam, the separate shrine of the goddess and the usual attendant deities. The sacred tree is the kondrai, the golden-flowered Indian laburnum dear to Shiva, and the temple's sacred water is the Vaigai itself, a few steps away.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of the Pandya king Cholanthakan, who would not take food before worshipping Shiva. Stranded one day far from any shrine and faint with hunger, he was shown by a minister a wooden wedge, an aappu, and told it was a lingam. The king worshipped it in good faith, and Shiva came to dwell in it — hence Appudaiyar, the Lord of the wedge. Another tale names him Annavinodhar: in a famine, the Lord told his priest to cook the sand of the Vaigai, and it turned to rice for the offering.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva year of Madurai: monthly Pradosham, Maha Shivaratri in Masi, Arudra Darshanam in Margazhi, and the Navaratri days of the goddess. The great city festivals of the Meenakshi temple also fill the riverside streets around Sellur. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Coming from the crowds of the Meenakshi temple, the walk across the Vaigai to Sellur feels like stepping into a quieter Madurai. Pause at the gateway to see Shiva and Parvati on the bull, worship the Lord who honoured a king's simple faith in a piece of wood, and visit the goddess of the fragrant tresses in her own shrine.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most Madurai temples. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Sellur is in north Madurai, just across the Vaigai from Simmakkal and about 2 km from the Meenakshi temple; city buses, autos and cabs reach it easily. Madurai Junction is the nearest railway station, and Madurai Airport lies about 15 km to the south.
